items.title: Your Policyholder Has an AI Agent, Too
items.original_title: Your Policyholder Has an AI Agent, Too
items.rss_title: Your Policyholder Has an AI Agent, Too
items.rss_description: Your Policyholder Has an AI Agent, Too AI & Machine Learning ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/28/2026 - 16:09 Life insurers are AI. The next challenge is preparing for policyholders who use AI to understand, question and optimize their policies. November 5, 2026 Image Imagine the customer of a 20-year-old life insurance policy trying to figure out if it makes sense to surrender the policy. Do they call the insurance company first, hoping to talk to a knowledgeable agent? Probably not. They will upload the policy contract, riders and most recent statement to the AI assistant with a list of questions: What benefits would be lost by surrendering the policy? What happens to the outstanding loans? Are there other alternatives to surrendering the policy? Which policy provisions are the most important to consider before deciding? This AI might be right, or might be partly right, or might be very wrong. But what is becoming abundantly clear is that this customer arrives at their insurer with a level of analysis and a body of knowledge that once cost time, or cost money, or both. This leads me back to the question insurers have been asking for years about how AI will change what we do: underwriting, servicing, operations, all inside the enterprise. So what happens when the policyholder is AI-enabled as well? The information gap is starting to change The Society of Actuaries Research Institute is now seeking research on policyholder behavior in the artificial intelligence era. According to the proposal request, it is possible for consumers to use AI to understand a policy's provisions better to improve their premiums, loans and withdrawals, and claims through improved product features. That isn't proof that AI has changed lapse rates, loan behavior, or benefit usage yet. It's on the research agenda. The difference is significant. But the formal asking of such questions by the actuarial community indicates that consumer AI requires attention before the results become apparent in experience studies. Up until recently, this has created a bit of a predicament: an insurer has product specialists, actuaries, underwriters, policy administration systems, and decades of institutional knowledge; a policyholder has a lengthy contract written in technical language and maybe the occasion to review it a couple of times. Generative AI won't remove that imbalance entirely, but it certainly lowers the cost of asking sophisticated questions about a complex contract. That alone changes the dynamic of that interaction. A long-lived contract can meet a very different customer Life insurance is unique because the contract could go on for decades, and the technology available to the user would be different from the present one. A policy issued in the age of paper statements and telephone calls may one day be managed by a consumer carrying a persistence layer of AI that summarizes documents, compares alternatives, remembers every previous conversation, and prepares detailed questions before every interaction. The policy's bones haven't altered one bit. But a policyholder's ability to kick the tires and check them out has. All this matters because many decisions and actions can occur throughout the lifecycle of a single life insurance policy: premium payment policy, loans, withdrawals, changes of beneficiary, conversion, surrender, and more. By making those decisions easier to understand and execute throughout the life of the product, there's no guarantee that customer behavior in the future will continue to be like the historical behaviors that informed product assumptions. Policyholder behavior may become an AI issue SOA's current research request explicitly identifies potential effects on lapses, loans, withdrawals, and benefit usage. A separate 2026 SOA call for essays on AI and the potential for antiselection in life insurance distribution asks whether AI could help applicants or intermediaries anticipate underwriting outcomes, compare carriers, select underwriting pathways and apply sophisticated placement strategies at greater scale. Once more, these are questions under investigation, not established outcomes. But, one thing appears clear: certain presumptions in life insurance are based on how people behave. Making it easier to evaluate the timing and consequences of a lapse, loan, withdrawal, conversion, surrender, or benefit election changes behavior in ways that historical behavior doesn't predict. The negative reaction to that realization is to predict material disruption. The right reaction is to begin measuring whether AI-assisted behavior is emerging, where it's concentrated, and if it's big enough to matter. From a more strategic perspective, for our actuarial and product teams, consumer AI could one day become another behavioral variable to study, rather than just a way to service customers better. AI-enabled policyholders can also be good for insurers This should not be framed only as a new risk. When a customer understands the policy, it allows them to ask the right questions, know what benefits they have, prepare the right documents, and know what decision they are making. Beneficiaries will use AI to organize materials for a claim, point out relevant policy language, and understand what the insurer is asking for. A policyholder who walks up to the window to service their policy will know the difference between a loan, withdrawal, and a surrender. This is consistent with the financial services research. In July 2026, LIMRA reported that AI is increasingly being studied not only as a tool that assists advisors but as a potential source of analysis and financial guidance directly to consumers. While more knowledgeable buyers are good for insurers, they also bring heightened expectations. A customer who has just received an instantaneous explanation of a policy provision may be less patient about waiting for days to get a generic response from a service agent. The customer's AI is not the insurer's AI Yet there is a boundary—the policyholder's AI is outside of the insurer's control. The model was not chosen, trained, fed, or even provided with its system prompt by the insurer. Your AI could be reading an outdated contract, skipping an endorsement, not grasping a rider, getting guaranteed vs. non-guaranteed values mixed up, or just making up a provision out of whole cloth that does not exist. The assertion could be false, or at least inaccurate. The enterprise response is to make verifying what the authoritative policy information says more accessible. Suppose a customer says, "My AI says this rider gives me a different option." It should be easy for a service person to say, "Let's review what your current contract and its effective endorsements, transaction history, and applicable rules say about this." The more external AI becomes part of customer decision-making, the more valuable clear, accessible, and authoritative policy context becomes. Soon, the customer may send the AI instead The next step is not difficult to imagine: the policyholder does not merely use AI before contacting the insurer. The AI contacts the insurer. That scenario is beginning to appear in insurance discussions already. An October 2026 Insurance Thought Leadership article described consumer AI agents calling insurers and other businesses on behalf of users. At the same time, NIST is developing work around identity and authorization for software and AI agents as agent-to-agent interactions move from concept toward practical infrastructure. This brings us to a much bigger question for life insurers: what if a chatbot does work? How would your service channel know that it's talking to software working for a policyholder? What data could be returned through that channel? What happens when a customer AI and your system don't agree on a policy provision? When does it become important to switch the interaction over to a person? There's nothing in those two scenarios that necessitates banning the use of AI in customer service. It just means that we, as users of these services, will need to create different channels for them to go through. Build policyholder AI readiness Insurers do not need to predict exactly how fast consumer agents will mature, but they do need to prepare for the direction of travel. First, make authoritative policy context easier to retrieve and explain. A policyholder's AI will only be as useful as the documents and information it can access. Clear digital contracts, current riders, transaction history, and understandable definitions reduce the chance that outside AI starts from incomplete context. Next, test servicing journeys with customers being assisted by AI in mind. When customers arrive having 10 specific questions, they should not follow the same process as someone who has only general questions. Third, watch how behavior changes. Teams — actuarial, product, servicing — that rely on lapses, loans, withdrawals, conversions, benefit usage, and channel usage need to understand what constitutes a significant deviation. We want to avoid blaming AI if another force is at work. The goal is to build evidence that indicates that AI is a cause before rewriting our assumptions about behavior. Fourth, prepare digital channels for external agents. Identity, consent, disclosure and escalation will become practical. We do not want to automatically trust an outside agent. We do want to ensure legitimate customer assistance can reach us and not diminish customer protection. The next AI transformation may happen outside the insurer When asked about the insurance AI strategy, carriers invariably identify the same things: automated underwriting, automated servicing, automated claims, automated document processing, and automated decision support. However, when it comes to the impact of artificial intelligence on enhancing service innovation, customer capabilities are also affected. The increased understanding could allow them to compare things to other products, which could open them up to asking difficult questions. However, what I think we have not talked about and probably is an elephant in the room is that insurers are not going to be in control of all this. They can only prepare for it. Will the next phase of life insurance AI be defined by how intelligent the insurer becomes? Or by what happens when the policyholder becomes intelligent at machine speed? Bhargavi Vepuri

items.rss_description: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy PaulCarroll Mon, 11/02/2026 - 11:30 Bill Gates recently said he is using generative AI as part of the annual, two-week strategy session that determines how the Gates Foundation spends its next $10 billion. He'll be "taking the strategy notes and actually engaging in a dialogue with ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, and even having them talk with each other," he said. I don't have $10 billion that I'm considering how to spend, and you may not, either, but genAI has now improved to the point where it can at least be an aid in setting strategy at almost any level. An old boss, Mel Bergstein, used to say: "Strategy is what you don't do." The idea worked for Mel, who founded a consulting firm, Diamond Management & Technology Partners, that pioneered the notion of digital strategy in the mid-1990s. Chunka Mui and I took Mel's adage further in our book, "Billion Dollar Lessons," for which we had 20 researchers spend two years looking at 2,500 major failures to identify the warning signs. Our recommended solution boiled down to having a "devil's advocate" identify all the underlying assumptions for a strategy, to keep problems from being glossed over as an executive team rushed to realize the CEO's plan. GenAI, used right, can now do a pretty good job of filling that role for anyone. Let's have a look. Gates told the New York Times that, "i n a few of the reviews, we’ll actually have the A.I. sit in. In a few cases, we’ll tell it: Hey, only speak if we ask you. And then in a few other cases, we’ll say: Hey, if you hear something you think is wrong or you hear us thinking about, for example, what are these statistics? Please engage. So we’ve gone from it being a joke [when someone suggested using genAI a year ago] to it will be a peer — not making any final decisions, but it will be a peer in deep, complex strategic discussions, making a significant contribution." I'm not willing to go that far just yet, partly because I'd need to test the domain knowledge that the large language models have about a subtle, heavily regulated business like insurance and partly because genAI has shown itself to be a sycophant. The biggest, overarching pattern of failure that Chunka and I found in the research for " Billion Dollar Lessons " was that people were reluctant to point out obvious problems that could derail initiatives that had the imprimatur of the CEO, and we don't want to replace human sycophants with AI ones. But you can describe your strategy to an AI, then pepper it with questions, going deeper each time while demanding evidence for its thinking and insisting it be blunt. Let's say you're thinking of buying a company. You could start with a general question: What could go wrong? Then you probe. How will our competitors react? What if interest rates increase? The economy goes into recession? The war in Iran escalates? Will we actually be able to cross-sell to our customers? Will the efficiencies from scale be as great as we expect? Who's done something similar and had problems? What were the problems? And on and on and on. You can do the same exercise if you're thinking of a new line of business, a software overhaul, adopting AI chatbots — or if you want to explore the dangers of standing pat, of not undertaking a major initiative that is under consideration. Major corporations have staff do extensive analysis along the lines I'm suggesting and, in the case of a possible acquisition, draw on their investment banks for advice — but the bias is always toward acting. If the perception is that the CEO backs an idea, the staff strives to make it work, not to kill it. Investment banks only collect their hefty fees if the deal happens, so why would they recommend against it? When Chunka and I did a consulting project with a major company that was considering launching autonomous vehicles, we saw elaborate studies it had commissioned from consulting firms that said the robotaxi business was a slam dunk and that the first to enter would win big. That was more than eight years ago. It turned out, however, that the executives working on the AV project internally were aware of all the sorts of operational and safety issues that we've all seen play out and that have slowed the robotaxi rollout. Those concerns were brought to the surface in the interviews for our devil's advocate review. Warren Buffett used to set aside two, equal pots of money when asking investment banks for advice on possible acquisitions — one for a bank that argued in favor of a deal and one for a bank that argued against it. Whichever carried the day collected its fees, while the other got nothing. You can be sure the "anti" bank worked as hard as possible on its arguments and evidence. In my experience, many big ideas should fall apart at the slightest scrutiny. As we wrote in "Billion Dollar Lessons," we thought 47% of the failures we investigated were based on strategies that never should have made it out of the strategy room — and not because those involved were stupid or inexperienced. The fifth-biggest cement maker in the world reasoned that it was really in the home products business because so much of its cement was used there. It began also making furnaces and lawn mowers... then went bankrupt and was bought by a competitor. Avon decided that its core competency was its culture of caring — not, you know, its line of cosmetics and its devoted salesforce — so it bought a maker of medical equipment and an operator of retirement homes. It had no idea how to operate the new businesses and quickly sold them at a major loss. In the early days of fax machines, FedEx spent hundreds of millions of dollars to set up a business that would collect a document from you, drive it to the nearest office, fax it to the office nearest your destination, then drive the fax to the recipient. The company somehow missed that Moore's law would soon make the devices so inexpensive that every company would have its own. It may take time to learn how to use genAI to avoid costly strategic mistakes — and that's even before we start using it as broadly as Gates is planning to. You'll likely also need to introduce to the LLM information specific to your market, including regulatory issues that it likely doesn't have even as these models try to Hoover up everything available on the internet. Insurance is a complicated market. But I think we're now at the point where genAI can, if managed correctly, start to catch strategic errors. We won't get that 47% figure for obviously bad ideas down to zero, but even heading toward 40%, maybe even 33%, would mark real progress. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll At any level of setting strategy, from the boardroom to the one-person agency, generative AI can bring assumptions to the surface, helping you see what NOT to do. items.rss_description: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating RyanMeyer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:00 ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims gets the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims gets the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? items.title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.original_title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.rss_title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.rss_description: Why Can't We Fund Prevention? Predict & Prevent ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/04/2026 - 09:29 Industrial organizations excel at financing recovery from asset failures but struggle to justify prevention spending with the same economic rigor. November 5, 2026 Image We've built an extraordinarily sophisticated financial system around industrial failure. We can price it, insure it, reserve capital for it, and finance recovery when it happens, but preventing that same failure often requires an entirely different standard of proof. Insurance is exceptionally good at mobilizing money after something goes wrong. Natural catastrophes caused an estimated $100 billion in economic losses in the first half of 2026. Insurance covered approximately 42%, leaving nearly $60 billion to be absorbed elsewhere. Insurance's ability to fund recovery is indispensable. The shortfall also exposes a contradiction in how risk is funded. Premiums, deductibles, and recovery costs have established places in corporate budgets. A proposal to prevent an asset failure faces a tougher test. Someone must prove the threat is serious, determine what intervention it warrants, and defend spending money on an event that might never happen. Failure has a funding mechanism. Prevention has a business case to make. Insurance can transfer part of a financial loss. It cannot restore missed production, repair damaged customer relationships, or undo the wider consequences of an industrial disruption. The challenge is making prevention as intelligible and investable as recovery. Knowing the risk isn't the same as managing it Industrial organizations rarely lack information. They receive risk-engineering reports, inspection findings, maintenance records and alerts from connected equipment. Yet information doesn't guarantee action. A temperature change, unusual vibration, or a deteriorating component has little meaning in isolation. Its significance depends on the asset's role in the operation. Is there redundancy? What production depends on it? What would a shutdown cost? Could a failure disrupt customers, supply chains or other facilities? These questions turn technical observations into business consequences. Without that translation, recommendations can remain in reports while maintenance teams address more immediate demands and capital committees fund projects with clearer returns. Industry has invested heavily in detecting changing conditions and predicting potential failures. Those capabilities matter. Still, knowing what might fail doesn't tell an organization which emerging risks deserve attention first. A relatively minor condition on a critical asset may represent far greater exposure than a severe condition on equipment with sufficient redundancy. The challenge is understanding what matters most, what the consequences could be, and where intervention will create the greatest value. Prevention needs to compete for capital Consider a manufacturer that identifies deterioration in a critical component on its main production line. Although the component hasn't failed, its condition is changing. The organization must compare the cost of replacing it during a planned shutdown with the lost output, repair time, and disruption that could follow an unplanned failure. The consequences, however, may extend well beyond that production line. A shutdown could affect customer deliveries, contractual commitments, supply-chain continuity and financial performance. What appears to be a maintenance decision may represent a much larger business risk. The appropriate response might be immediate repair, closer monitoring, a change in operating parameters or acceptance of the exposure. Someone must have the authority to make that decision and commit the necessary resources before the opportunity to intervene passes. Now multiply that challenge across hundreds of assets and facilities, each presenting different levels of exposure. The question is no longer simply whether an individual intervention is justified. It's which interventions deserve priority when resources are limited, and the consequences extend across the enterprise. For decades, industry has developed sophisticated ways to measure losses after they occur. We need comparable discipline in understanding the economic value of preventing those losses before they happen. Capital should not only be deployed to absorb loss. It should be possible to direct it intelligently toward preventing loss. The standard for resilience must rise Risk assessments, inspections and engineering recommendations are essential. Completing those processes, however, doesn't necessarily mean an organization has addressed its most consequential exposures. An inspection can establish that a process was followed. A risk assessment can document a vulnerability. Neither, by itself, demonstrates that the organization is becoming more resilient. Industrial risk isn't static. Asset conditions change, operational dependencies evolve, and an exposure that appeared manageable during a periodic assessment may become significantly more consequential. A recommendation without a named decision-maker and deadline is information, not control. Someone must have the authority to accept the exposure, fund the response or explain why another course is justified. Following the process is important, although it's not the same as preventing the loss. Insurance can help change the economics of prevention Insurers can make recommendations easier to act on by explaining the severity and urgency of an exposure, not simply recording that it exists. Brokers can connect risk-engineering findings with an organization's insurance and resilience priorities. Operators must determine whether to intervene or accept the exposure and take responsibility for the outcome. There is also a bigger opportunity here. Insurers and brokers possess extraordinary expertise in understanding, quantifying, and pricing risk. Much of that expertise has historically helped organizations prepare financially for potential losses. What if more of it could be applied to making prevention economically compelling before those losses occur? Imagine insurers, brokers, and industrial operators working from a more continuous, consequence-based understanding of emerging physical risk. Rather than relying primarily on historical losses and periodic assessments, they could better understand where exposure is developing, which conditions present the greatest business consequences, and where intervention could materially reduce risk. This wouldn't eliminate uncertainty or diminish the need for insurance. It could, however, create a stronger economic foundation for prevention and a more productive relationship between risk financing and operational decision-making. For decades, the insurance industry has helped businesses understand the financial consequences of what can go wrong. That expertise will remain indispensable, but the next opportunity is to help make the economics of what doesn't have to go wrong equally visible. We've become extraordinarily good at financing industrial failure. It's time to become just as disciplined about investing in its prevention. Andy Pruett

items.rss_description: Demo: AI Agent for P&C Claims Coverage Verification Insurtech in Action: The ITL Demos RyanMeyer Wed, 11/04/2026 - 09:42 ScienceSoft's agentic solution matches P&C claim details against policy documents and delivers evidence-backed coverage conclusions in minutes while keeping adjusters in control of final decisions November 4, 2026 Watch Our Demo: Why We Are the Right Solution For Your Needs ScienceSoft's AI Agent for P&C Claims Coverage Verification adapts to your existing operations and technology landscape rather than forcing you to work around the software. Comes ready for coverage verification. The agent can automate the end-to-end workflow out of the box, from policy research and coverage analysis to evidence-backed memos and reservation of rights letters. Fits your claims processes and rules. ScienceSoft can customize the agent's verification logic, workflows, and outputs to reflect your coverage policies, authority levels, and claims handling practices. Lets you set the boundaries for AI. Built-in controls allow you to define which findings require human review, when the agent should escalate a case, and how AI-generated conclusions are validated. Works with your existing systems. The solution can integrate with commercial claims platforms and legacy applications without limiting your technology stack. You can deploy it in your cloud or on-premises environment. Watch the demo to see the agent verify coverage for a homeowners hail damage claim. Main Benefits of Our Product: Faster coverage verification. In early tests, the AI agent helped cut coverage verification time from 2–3 days to just 30 minutes by automating policy analysis and document preparation. Greater claims team capacity. items.extracted_text: Allstate’s AI Ecosystem to Include a Personal Agentic Assistant for Customers Article 0 Comments The next stop in Allstate’s journey with artificial intelligence – a personal agentic assistant for consumers. CEO Tom Wilson revealed that customers could expect an Allstate PAA early in 2027. He said the PAA has been in development for more than a year. “The foundational technology is in place…the algorithms are being tested,” he said. Related: Allstate Q3 Net Income Drops About 45% on Higher Catastrophe Losses “We want to give customers more value every day in as many ways as we can, including leveraging technology, and having a PAA will enable more people to come to us,” Wilson said during an earnings with analysts. “If they don’t feel like calling an Allstate agent – or feel like getting on our website – and they just want to have a PAA do that, we’re fine with that.” Wilson Wilson said personal lines new business is up 125% over 2019, and currently split about eventually between exclusive agents, independent agents, and direct-to-consumer. However, the advent of PAAs “gives us the opportunity to serve consumers who prefer to have a machine to handle their transactions,” Wilson added. Allstate said it does not yet have a name for its PAA, but it will leverage Allstate’s Large Language Intelligent Ecosystem (ALLIE), which is ingesting code at a much high rate than just a few months ago. The insurer has already launched a customer service agent called Ask Allstate, which handles a variety of inquiries for customers. Allstate said its PAA will also work with existing PAAs, such as Muse. Related: Allstate Introduces Large Language Model, ALLIE “Essentially, we’re now marketing to machines and people, not just marketing to people,” Wilson explained. “These capabilities also give us the opportunity to be offensive in leveraging capabilities by launching a PAA that’s an expert in protection that still meets consumers’ needs and their desires for fewer clicks.” The PAA will additionally provide context on coverage needs of the customer, he added. Wilson said the speed of the development of this market is unclear, but getting in now “will enable Allstate to provide increased value for customers.” “We believe that this will actually help the existing PAAs out there,” Wilson said. When asked about possible regulatory or cyber concerns, Wilson added that Allstate will “figure out stuff like what do we do with the regulators, what do we do with privacy, what do we do with cybersecurity, as we go.” “There’s work to be done, but the benefit to customers and the economic rationale is going to move this train down the path,” Wilson said. “This is going to happen. So we decided to get in on it, accelerate it, go as fast as we can, which is why we started leaning into the PAA.” Was this article valuable? Yes No Here are more articles you may enjoy. items.extracted_text: ICE to launch European wind futures in weather derivatives expansion - Artemis.bm ICE to launch European wind futures in weather derivatives expansion - Artemis.bm ICE to launch European wind futures in weather derivatives expansion 9th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Intercontinental Exchange, Inc. (ICE) a provider of financial market technology and data powering global capital markets, is launching 15 cash-settled wind futures contracts in December, which will expand its energy offerings into weather derivatives to cover wind generation across seven different European countries. Set to launch on December 14th, 2026, subject to completion of relevant regulatory processes, the contracts are based on wind power output indices published by ENWEX GmbH (ENWEX), a provider of weather and renewable energy indices for temperature, wind and solar. As mentioned, seven European countries will be covered by the new contracts, including Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and the U.K. ICE has confirmed that the new contracts will cover onshore wind (turbines on land), offshore wind (turbines at sea) and the two combined, depending on the country. In addition, ICE also noted that the seven countries covered by the new contracts account for over 70% of Europe’s total installed wind generation capacity. Combined with ICE’s European power futures, the contracts will also reportedly allow wind producers, utilities, suppliers and buyers under power purchase agreements to manage the volume risk of wind generation as well as the price risk of electricity. It’s also important to add, that with these being weather derivative instruments, we can assume that these will involve either parametric or weather index trigger contracts. Gordon Bennett, Managing Director, Utility Markets at ICE, commented: “Climatic variable futures are a natural addition to the energy markets we already offer. Wind volume is now a significant part of the power sector, and customers want a way to manage it alongside what they already trade with us. Our energy and environmental portfolio allow participants to hedge across commodities, hubs and time periods, and to manage the links between natural gas, power and carbon in one place.” Bennett added: “Because the amount of wind generated affects how much gas-fired power is needed, wind futures give customers a way to manage exposures that run through all three, with the same trading and clearing relationships they already have with ICE.” Robin Girmes, Managing Director at ENWEX, said: “As renewable generation grows, managing weather-driven volume risk is increasingly essential, particularly in the expanding market for renewable power purchase agreements. “We believe transparent, standardized and independently calculated indices are fundamental to making renewable energy generation risks measurable, tradable and hedgeable. We are proud that ICE has chosen ENWEX indices as the foundation for these new wind contracts, a step towards establishing weather risk as an integral part of modern energy markets.” Back in August we reported that the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME Group) is also expanding its range of weather risk transfer and hedging products, with a plan to launch Wind Power futures and options based on indices provided by Vaisala Xweather later this year . Hedging weather variability enables volatility to be mitigated and earnings to be smoothed for the renewable energy industry, a key use of weather derivatives and weather futures or option contracts. Being index-based risk transfer and hedging products, these are technically parametric in nature. In the past we’ve seen ILS investment managers allocating capital to weather derivatives markets, as a complementary asset to the more traditional natural catastrophe reinsurance contracts they typically invest in. items.extracted_text: Global Parametrics to design Peru’s first parametric earthquake insurance solution - Artemis.bm Global Parametrics to design Peru’s first parametric earthquake insurance solution - Artemis.bm Global Parametrics to design Peru’s first parametric earthquake insurance solution 9th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Global Parametrics (part of CelsiusPro Group), has announced the development and planned pilot of Peru’s first parametric earthquake insurance product, specifically designed to help protect 17,000 low-income household members against earthquake risk in Lima, Peru. The parametric product, which will be supported through the Natural Disaster Fund’s (NDF) Technical Assistance Facility (TAF) grant, will help safeguard livelihoods and mitigate the longer-term impact of earthquakes on employment and household incomes across Lima. The pilot aims to protect 5,000 vulnerable policyholders, supporting approximately 17,000 household members, primarily based in low-income and progressive housing. According to the announcement, this will lay the groundwork to scaling the product to up to 20,000 policyholders in its second year and for expansion beyond Lima. The product will initially have a key focus on Lima, where Global Parametrics, in partnership with MicroInsurance Centre at Milliman, Three Fin Consulting, Swisscontact, La Positiva Seguros and local microfinance institutions, will be able to work closely with local stakeholders, monitor implementation and assess the effectiveness of the product before scaling. Moreover, Global Parametrics explained that partnering with Swisscontact Peru supports a more holistic approach to resilience building, providing further support to progressive housing homeowners through risk reduction activities, including capacity building for local builders. Mark Rueegg, Founder and CEO of CelsiusPro Group, commented: “Delivering this pilot initiative in Peru marks the first signed NDF TAF grant contract signed since the replenishment of the TAF by the UK Government’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) announced in June. He continued: “Piloting this parametric insurance product against earthquake risk will demonstrate how innovative risk transfer solutions can provide greater financial stability for vulnerable households. By combining data with local expertise, we are developing practical solutions that can help close the protection gap and build greater resilience to natural hazards.” Peru is highly vulnerable to earthquake risk, as it lies in one of the world’s most seismically active regions along the convergent plate boundary between the Nazca and South American Plates. In addition, low-income households are especially vulnerable to the financial impacts of earthquakes. Having limited access to appropriate risk management tools, along with housing informality and the fact that the locations of many homes happen to be located in highly seismic areas can make it increasingly difficult for traditional insurers to provide affordable coverage for vulnerable households. As a result, this parametric solution being developed by the NDF will offer further ways to extend protection to these vulnerable households, including those without formal property titles. In addition, the parametric quake product will also be tailored to livelihood protection, recognising that the financial impact of an earthquake can extend beyond physical damage to homes and assets. By providing financial support following a qualifying seismic event, the solution aims to help households manage immediate costs and reduce the potential disruption to employment and household incomes. John Caroll, Consultant and Latin America Specialist for the MicroInsurance Centre, said: “We will integrate customercentric design at every stage of product development and piloting, incorporating input and validation from the target market throughout the process. We intend to engage in co-design approaches with our consortium partners. We are encouraged by our partners’ dedication in the lead-up to the pilot launch and are confident that, together, we can design a valuable and sustainable solution to protect low-income households and those living in progressive housing.” Swisscontact Chairman, Thomas Meyer, added: “Our partnership with Global Parametrics, alongside our Vivienda Progressiva (VIPRO) Program, will link insurance to our risk reduction programmes, combining financial resilience with measures designed to reduce exposure to earthquake risk. Peru is a vital location for this work: according to CENEPRED (2025), over 14.8 million people and 4.6 million homes face very high seismic risk. By combining financial protection with practical risk reduction measures, we can help vulnerable households and local communities prepare for and recover from the impact of earthquakes.” Lourdes del Carpio, Agrarian Insurance Manager at La Positiva Seguros, noted: “The evolution of the insurance sector depends on our ability to keep developing solutions that respond to the country’s changing protection needs. At La Positiva, we see innovation as an ongoing commitment to expanding the possibilities of insurance and reaching new segments. This initiative allows us to explore further applications of parametric insurance in Peru and contribute to the development of solutions tailored to the needs of families living in progressive housing.” The Natural Disaster Fund (NDF) was launched back in 2018 by Global Parametrics and was seeded by the UK’s Department for International Development (DFID) later on that same year. items.extracted_text: Tesla to Phase Out Cybertruck After Years of Poor Sales Article 0 Comments Tesla Inc. is discontinuing the Cybertruck, the polarizing pickup that turned plenty of heads in its brief time on the market but never sold anywhere near Elon Musk’s lofty predictions. Production will wind down at Tesla’s Texas plant in the middle of next year to free up capacity for the Cybercab autonomous vehicle, Musk said Friday in a social-media post that didn’t offer further details. The chief executive officer confirmed the cancellation in a subsequent post on X in which he said he still expected a fleet of Cybertrucks to be around “for a long time.” Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 6, 2026 The abrupt announcement amounts to a death knell for the divisive electric truck, which fell well short of demand projections and suffered a series of recalls. Bloomberg News reported earlier this year that sales had been propped up by purchases from Musk’s other companies, particularly SpaceX. The phase-out in part reflects the Cybertruck’s “relatively limited commercial success,” Barclays analyst Dan Levy said in a note. Tesla is making about 20,000 of the pickups a year, roughly 1% of the company’s total volume and a fraction of the more than 125,000 that the factory is capable of producing, he said. The angular and unconventional vehicle divided opinion as soon as Musk unveiled a prototype in 2019. Tesla’s chief designer threw a metal ball at its supposedly shatter-proof window on stage, only for the glass to break. Tesla began building Cybertrucks at its factory near Austin in 2023, when Musk estimated Tesla might make more than 250,000 annually, depending on demand. The company sold less than one-sixth that number in its first year. Musk nevertheless extolled the pickup earlier this year as “the best vehicle Tesla has ever made.” Wes Morrill, Tesla’s lead Cybertruck engineer, thanked buyers and Tesla workers in a post Friday on X, saying the model “was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab.” Killing the Cybertruck extends a trend in which Tesla prunes the more expensive and slower-selling models from its already-slim lineup. The automaker discontinued its pricey Model S and X vehicles earlier this year. The vast majority of its sales come from the Model Y SUV and Model 3 sedan. A Tesla Cybercab prototype on display last year in New York. Last quarter, Tesla reported that it sold 8,295 “other models,” most of which likely were Cybertrucks. That was down sharply from a year ago, when the US still offered a federal EV tax credit and when the now-discontinued Model S and Model X were included in the category. Tesla shares rose 3.1% as of 9:50 a.m. in New York, rebounding modestly from declines following the US midterm elections. Tesla has been deemphasizing its core auto business in recent quarters, and investors have largely looked past sales results as Musk works to refocus on futuristic business lines including AI, robotics and autonomous vehicles. Central to that effort is the Cybercab, a two-seat car with no steering wheel or foot pedals. The company began producing Cybercabs at the Austin factory this year and recently rolled it out for the public through Tesla’s robotaxi service. The car already is under scrutiny: U.S. auto-safety regulators are probing the process and technical data Tesla relied on when the company self-certified the vehicles as compliant with all federal safety standards. items.extracted_text: GSK, Moderna Settle Patent Dispute Over Moderna COVID, RSV Shots Article 0 Comments British drugmaker GSK has settled lawsuits that accused Moderna’s COVID-19 vaccines Spikevax and mNEXSPIKE and RSV shot mResvia of infringing its patents, the companies said on Friday. Moderna said in a Friday press release that it settled GSK’s patent litigation in the U.S. and Europe on October 28 and that the companies “granted patent cross-licenses in the field of infectious disease and are not obligated to make payments of any kind in connection with such licenses.” A GSK spokesperson said the company was “pleased to have reached a resolution that provides clarity for both companies and enables continued focus on advancing innovation for patients.” The companies asked a Delaware federal court on Friday to dismiss GSK’s US infringement claims with prejudice, which means they cannot be refiled GSK sued Moderna in 2024 over lipid nanoparticle technology used in the vaccines to transport fragile messenger RNA (mRNA) into the human body GSK separately filed a similar lawsuit against Pfizer and BioNTech over their COVID-19 vaccine earlier that year, which is still ongoing The lawsuits are part of a web of U.S. court cases involving Pfizer, BioNTech and Moderna over patent royalties for technology used in their COVID vaccines, including one brought by Moderna against Pfizer in 2022 (Reporting by Brittain in Washington Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi) Copyright 2026 Reuters. items.extracted_text: Investors Settle With KPMG Over Silicon Valley Bank Collapse Article 0 Comments Investors involved in a class action lawsuit over the 2023 collapse of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) have reached a $224.5 million settlement with external auditor KPMG LLP, Norway’s sovereign wealth fund said on Friday. KPMG said the settlement was not an admission of wrongdoing and that it stood by its work. SVB’s collapse in March 2023 was the trigger for the worst banking shock since the 2008 global financial crisis, affecting bank stocks globally. The Norwegian fund later said the case raised significant concerns regarding the integrity of the public markets, the governance of large financial institutions and the interests of the investor community more broadly. “The settlement is an important first step toward recovering investor losses from one of the largest bank failures in U.S. history,” Nicolai Tangen, CEO of the Norwegian sovereign wealth fund, said in a statement. “We continue to stand by our audits of Silicon Valley Bank, and we are proud of our audit quality track record. This settlement is a strategic decision to move forward as a business. It is not an admission of any wrongdoing,” a KPMG U.S. spokesperson said in a written statement. The class action case continues against other defendants, the Norwegian fund said. The fund, which invests Norway’s surplus oil and gas revenue abroad, is the world’s biggest single stock market investor, owning some 1.5% of all globally listed shares with stakes in more than 7,000 companies. It held a 1% stake in SVB at the end of 2022, valued at $137.9 million, according to data on the fund’s website. items.extracted_text: VKB seeks reduced pricing for King Max Re German multi-peril cat bond renewal - Artemis.bm VKB seeks reduced pricing for King Max Re German multi-peril cat bond renewal - Artemis.bm VKB seeks reduced pricing for King Max Re German multi-peril cat bond renewal 9th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans German domestic market insurance group VKB is now aiming to secure its first renewal of a catastrophe bond at reduced pricing, with the price guidance now lowered for the still €175 million King Max Re II DAC (Series 2026-1) German multi-peril transaction, we understand from sources. Versicherungskammer Bayern Versicherungsanstalt des oeffentlichen Rechts’ (VKB) returned to the catastrophe bond market for its second sponsorship in October, with the transaction a renewal of sorts for its soon to mature debut issuance. The company had sponsored its debut cat bond in late 2023, securing €175 million of multi-peril catastrophe reinsurance protection from the King Max Re DAC 2023 issuance, which is scheduled to mature in early January 2027. This renewal transaction comes with a lower attachment point than the maturing cat bond, showing VKB looking to bring the protection further down within its reinsurance tower. The initial size target for this of King Max Re II Series 2026-1 Class A notes has not changed, being still for €175 million of reinsurance, so to fully replace the expiring cat bond protection. The €175 million of King Max Re II Series 2026-1 Class A notes are designed to provide sponsoring reinsurer VKB Re with indemnity and per-occurrence triggered reinsurance protection against losses from the perils of earthquake, hailstorm, flood and windstorm in Germany, over a three year term beginning January 1st 2027. These King Max Re II Series 2026-1 Class A cat bond notes come with an initial expected loss of 1.68% and were first offered to investors with price guidance for a spread of between 3% and 3.25%. We’re now told that the price guidance has been revised at a lower level, with an updated range for a spread of between 2.5% and 3%. Once again, VKB looks set to be another sponsor that benefits from the strong execution being seen in the catastrophe bond market, now on-track to secure its renewal issuance at the low-end of initial price guidance or below. items.extracted_text: Avec 11,5 milliards d’euros de cotisations en août 2026, l’assurance vie demeure un levier essentiel pour financer l’économie française et européenne - France Assureurs À 11,5 milliards d’euros, les cotisations en assurance vie sont en baisse de −6 % en août 2026 par rapport au même mois de 2025. Les prestations du mois d’août 2026 s’élèvent à 9,5 milliards d’euros, en hausse de +15 % par rapport à août 2025. Elles atteignent ainsi leur plus haut niveau depuis trois ans pour un mois d’août. La collecte nette s’établit à +2,0 milliards d’euros, en baisse de −1,9 milliard d’euros par rapport à celle d’août 2025. Depuis le début de l’année, elle s’élève à +43,5 milliards d’euros, supérieure de +6,9 milliards d’euros à celle de 2025 sur la même période. En août 2026, les cotisations en assurance vie s’élèvent à 11,5 milliards d’euros, en diminution de −6 % par rapport au même mois de 2025 où les cotisations avaient atteint un niveau exceptionnellement élevé (12,2 milliards d’euros, soit +27 % par rapport à août 2024). Les cotisations progressent de +3 % pour les supports en unités de compte (UC) mais diminuent pour les supports en euros (−10 %). Depuis début 2026, les cotisations atteignent 138,7 milliards d’euros, en hausse de +9,2 milliards d’euros, soit +7 % par rapport aux huit premiers mois de 2025. Cette dynamique positive concerne principalement les supports en UC (+10 %) et dans une moindre mesure ceux en euros (+5 %). La part des UC dans les cotisations s’établit à 37 % sur le mois d’août 2026 et se maintient à 40 % sur les huit premiers mois de l’année. À 9,5 milliards d’euros, les prestations du mois d’août 2026 sont en hausse de +15 % par rapport à août 2025. Cette augmentation est portée essentiellement par les supports en UC (+27 %), tandis que ceux en euros enregistrent une hausse de +11 %. Les prestations atteignent ainsi leur plus haut niveau pour un mois d’août depuis trois ans, avec notamment 2,4 milliards d’euros de prestations sur les supports en UC. Depuis le début de l’année, les prestations s’élèvent à 95,2 milliards d’euros, en légère progression de +2,3 milliards d’euros, soit +2 % par rapport aux huit premiers mois de 2025. Cette dynamique concerne principalement les supports en UC qui augmentent de +1,5 milliard d’euros, tandis que les prestations des supports en euros sont en hausse de +0,8 milliard d’euros. La collecte nette s’établit donc à +2,0 milliards d’euros en août 2026. Les supports en UC représentent l’essentiel de cette dynamique, avec une collecte nette positive de +1,9 milliard d’euros, tandis que les supports en euros enregistrent une collecte positive de +0,2 milliard d’euros. Depuis le début de l’année, la collecte nette s’élève à +43,5 milliards d’euros, supérieure de +6,9 milliards d’euros à celle de 2025 sur la même période. Les supports en UC concentrent une partie très majoritaire de cette collecte nette (+33,9 milliards d’euros), tandis que ceux en euros y contribuent à hauteur de +9,7 milliards d’euros. L’encours des contrats d’assurance vie atteint 2 171 milliards d’euros à fin août 2026, en hausse de +5,7 % sur un an (+117 milliards d’euros). Selon Paul ESMEIN, directeur général de France Assureurs : «En août 2026, les cotisations en assurance vie demeurent à un niveau élevé, à 11,5 milliards d’euros. Depuis le début de l’année, la dynamique de l’assurance vie confirme la confiance des Français dans ce produit d’épargne de long terme, qui leur permet de préparer leur avenir, tout en contribuant au financement de l’économie française. Avec 80 % de ses encours investis au sein de l’Union européenne et plus de la moitié sur le territoire français, l’assurance vie constitue un levier essentiel au service de la souveraineté nationale et européenne. » Pour en savoir plus sur l’assurance vie, cliquez ici. NB : l’arrondi d’un total ou d’une différence n’est pas nécessairement égal à la somme ou à la différence des arrondis de ses composantes. C’est parfois le cas entre la collecte nette d’une part et la différence entre les cotisations et les prestations d’autre part, lorsque ces grandeurs sont toutes trois arrondies en milliards d’euros. items.extracted_text: Illinois Roofing Company to Pay $700K in Race and Sex Harassment Suit Article 0 Comments Anthony Roofing Tecta America LLC, an Aurora, Illinois-based roofing company, will pay $700,000 and furnish other relief to settle a race and sex harassment lawsuit brought by the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), the federal agency announced. The EEOC suit asserted that one of Anthony Roofing’s vice presidents racially and sexually harassed multiple employees. This included repeatedly calling one employee the n-word and his “slave,” among other offensive racial remarks. The harassment continued even after the employee raised objections to such treatment. Left unaddressed, the harassment escalated — resulting in at least one instance of unwelcome physical contact, forcing the employee to quit to avoid further abuse. Multiple employees reported the race and sex harassment to management and human resources for Anthony Roofing, but the company failed to act, the lawsuit said. The alleged conduct violates Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits workplace harassment based on race and sex, as well as retaliating against individuals who oppose such harassment. items.title: Food Industry Pushes Back on WHO Guidance for Products With Added Color, Flavor
items.original_title: Food Industry Pushes Back on WHO Guidance for Products With Added Color, Flavor
items.rss_title: Food Industry Pushes Back on WHO Guidance for Products With Added Color, Flavor
items.rss_description: Governments should consider regulating foods that include added colors, flavors or sweeteners designed to make the product more appealing to consumers, according to new draft World Health Organization guidance that has sparked swift pushback from the food industry. The WHO …
items.extracted_text: Food Industry Pushes Back on WHO Guidance for Products With Added Color, Flavor Article 0 Comments Governments should consider regulating foods that include added colors, flavors or sweeteners designed to make the product more appealing to consumers, according to new draft World Health Organization guidance that has sparked swift pushback from the food industry. The WHO draft aims to help governments identify which foods should be consumed in moderation as part of a healthy diet – and which products could be subject to measures like warning labels or taxes, depending on national priorities. The new draft food-profiling model, published last week, marks the first time the UN health agency has included this type of ingredient in its guidance, previously only focused on nutritional content, including fat and salt. “This draft goes beyond traditional nutrient profiling by recognizing that foods may need to be considered not only for their nutrient content, but also for other aspects of their formulation” in order to prevent diet-related disease, said Katrin Engelhardt, technical officer at the WHO’s department of nutrition and food safety. Around 11 million deaths a year are linked to unhealthy diets, according to the agency, based on data from a global study. The proposed new model is also the WHO’s attempt to guide member states through an increasingly polarized debate about ultra-processed foods (UPFs), a class of food or drink made using processing techniques, additives and industrial ingredients, which often contain little whole food. Examples include carbonated soft drinks or instant noodles. Beyond Nutrients Alone Many food scientists say UPFs pose numerous health risks but others – and the food industry – say they are defined too widely, which risks demonizing healthy products. The International Food and Beverage Alliance, an organization representing major multinational food and beverage companies, said it was concerned the proposed approach shifts attention away from nutritional quality and could capture more products for potential regulation. “Of particular concern is the potential to undermine established nutrition priorities and reformulation efforts,” said IFBA Secretary General Rocco Renaldi. Other concerns for the food industry are higher costs from reformulating products or stringent labeling requirements, as well as the risk of class-action lawsuits as seen in the United States, and higher taxes for processed food companies. Broadly, the WHO said the model covers “industrially-produced foods to be consumed in moderation”, and is a bridge between its healthy diet recommendations and government policy on individual food products. Lindsey Smith Taillie, co-director of the Global Food Research Program at the University of Chapel Hill, North Carolina, said the point of the model was to target unhealthy foods, combining both nutrients and UPFs. “These two frameworks have never been mutually exclusive and can and should be used by policymakers as the starting place,” she said, adding that healthiness is measured by multiple criteria. Kraft Heinz CEO Steve Cahillane last week told Reuters that industry players should have a say. “We’re in the food business and we care about consumers deeply,” Cahillane said. “And so we ought to have a seat at the table as these discussions evolve.” The WHO proposal is out for consultation until November 27. items.extracted_text: Iowa Postal Worker Shot Two Co-Workers at Post Office, Police Say Article 0 Comments A female postal worker shot two female co-workers at the main post office in Iowa’s capital city Thursday before being captured nearby and faces attempted murder charges, authorities said. Jennifer Christine Pledger, 39, of West Des Moines, stood above one woman who she had shot and fired again, police said, and continued firing as she fled the building. A male employee was injured in a fall while trying to escape. None of the injuries were believed to be life-threatening, according to police. “They’re all at the hospital. They are being cared for right now,” Des Moines police Sgt. Paul Parizek said of the victims, who included two women, 45 and 53, and a 55-year-old man. All were in stable condition. Pledger is being charged with two counts of attempted murder, two counts of willful injury causing serious injury and intimidation. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach possible relatives were unsuccessful and information was not immediately available on an attorney who could speak on her behalf. The shooting happened on the facility’s second floor, in an area not accessible to the public. Witnesses reported hearing 10 to 12 shots, he said. Parizek said officers responded within three minutes and quickly captured Pledger, who was detained along a nearby bike path without resistance. A 9 mm handgun was recovered where she was detained. Police began receiving calls about the shooting around 9:10 a.m., and the suspect was detained at 9:21 a.m., Parizek said. The post office is just north of downtown Des Moines and across the street from one of the city’s main hospitals. A spokesperson for the U.S. Postal Inspection Service said in an email that it was investigating the shooting along with local, state and federal law enforcement. Gov. Kim Reynolds said she was in contact with the Department of Public Safety regarding the shooting. “We are monitoring the situation and our prayers are with everyone involved,” she posted online. “Grateful for the immediate response by law enforcement.” Des Moines Public Schools said the district’s nearby elementary school, welcome center and nutrition center temporarily barred anyone from entering or leaving the facilities due to the shooting. Those restrictions were lifted after police told them the suspect was in custody. Past shootings at postal facilities have prompted the Postal Service to study employee safety. In 1986, a disgruntled postal worker went on a deadly rampage at a post office in Edmond, Oklahoma, shooting 14 fellow workers before killing himself. In 1991, a fired postal worker killed four former co-workers at his former post office in Royal Oak, Michigan, before killing himself. After those and other shootings, postal officials commissioned a study released in 2000 to examine workplace violence around the time that the term “going postal” was becoming conversational. The report issued several recommendations to flag violent tendencies while concluding that “going postal” was a myth and that postal employees are less violent than the national workforce. Other attacks have occurred since the report, including a 2006 shooting in Goleta, California, where a former postal worker stormed into a sorting facility and fatally shot six workers before killing himself. ___ Associated Press writers R.J. items.rss_title: SpaceXAI Started Data Center Build Without Water Permits, Mississippi Says
items.rss_description: Mississippi’s environmental regulators released details this week on a set of penalties against SpaceXAI for violating state water pollution laws by starting construction on its Southaven data center facilities without needed permits. The company first announced the potential fines to …
items.extracted_text: SpaceXAI Started Data Center Build Without Water Permits, Mississippi Says Article 0 Comments Mississippi’s environmental regulators released details this week on a set of penalties against SpaceXAI for violating state water pollution laws by starting construction on its Southaven data center facilities without needed permits. The company first announced the potential fines to investors two weeks ago, speculating the amount could reach as much as $6.1 million. To limit pollution from construction reaching public bodies of water, state law requires companies to first obtain a permit. Without proper protections, rain runoff, for instance, can carry debris and chemicals off construction sites and pollute natural habitats, drinking water systems and recreational areas, federal regulators warn. Earlier this year, SpaceXAI – through its subsidiary, MZX Tech LLC – asked the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality for permits allowing construction within its growing Southaven footprint , which includes a power plant as well as land to build a $20 billion data center facility called MACROHARDERR. But during a July meeting between MDEQ and MZX Tech, “it became apparent” the company had already begun construction on the land in question, impacting about 30 acres, MDEQ records show. On July 16, a day after the meeting, MDEQ staff visited Southaven and confirmed the infractions. The agency sent two notices of violation to MZX Tech on Aug. 10, both of which “will be subject to the maximum statutory penalty” of $25,000 for each day construction continues without the needed permits, MDEQ wrote. “The Company is cooperating with MDEQ and is in discussions to resolve the matters through a single agreed order,” SpaceXAI wrote in its Oct. 22 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. It’s unclear where the $6.1 million figure came from. Based on the $25,000-per-day figure, it could suggest the violations lasted for several months. But MDEQ declined to say if the amount was accurate, citing its policy not to comment on pending enforcement matters. At one of the MZX Tech properties, a former Southaven training facility that neighbors Horn Lake Creek, MDEQ staff found that “no steps have been taken to protect stormwater infrastructure at the site,” and that there was a lack of protection against “fugitive dust emissions.” At the 2400 Stateline Road property, the site for MACROHARDERR, the staff found “no controls around storm inlets.” The MDEQ inspectors noted that, while construction appeared to have started around the beginning of 2026, the property’s last construction storm water permit expired in 2023. MDEQ Responds to Federal Judge About its Turbine Exemptions Last week, a federal judge found that MDEQ had misinterpreted federal clean air statutes when allowing SpaceXAI to run 69 temporary natural gas turbines without a permit. U.S. District Court Judge Debra Brown included the opinion in her ruling against a motion to dismiss the NAACP’s April lawsuit against the data center company. MDEQ relied on a federal Clean Air Act exemption intended for mobile generators, and SpaceXAI’s turbines clearly did not meet that criteria, Brown reasoned. That distinction is a key focus of the NAACP’s argument against the company. The agency responded to the order in a statement to Mississippi Today on Wednesday. “MDEQ is aware of the Court’s order and takes seriously all opinions by a federal court,” agency spokesperson Jan Schaefer said. “Nonetheless, MDEQ is not a party to that case and the order is not binding upon the agency. Furthermore, that litigation is ongoing and subject to appeal so it is not final at this point. “MDEQ always seeks to make sure our policies are in compliance with state and federal law and will do the same here once that litigation concludes.” The agency first told the Elon Musk-owned company last year that it could run the generators without a permit because the units are “affixed to a portable unit (i.e., a flatbed trailer)” and are therefore considered mobile. Brown, though, disagreed. She argued that, given the size of the generators and the fact they aren’t “self-propelled or intended to be propelled” while operating, the federal exemption for mobile sources can’t apply. This story was originally published by Mississippi Today and distributed through a partnership with The Associated Press. Top photo: The SpaceXAI power plant in Southaven in February. items.extracted_text: UCITS cat bond fund returns hit 7.87% YTD after October. 12-month declines again: Plenum Index - Artemis.bm UCITS cat bond fund returns hit 7.87% YTD after October. 12-month declines again: Plenum Index - Artemis.bm UCITS cat bond fund returns hit 7.87% YTD after October. 12-month declines again: Plenum Index 9th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Catastrophe bond funds structured as UCITS investment strategies delivered strong returns in October to end the month with a 7.87% return for 2026 so far, while the rolling-twelve month average performance has declined further, according to the Plenum CAT Bond UCITS Fund Indices . 2026 remains on-track to see at the least the fourth highest annual return for UCITS cat bond funds, according to specialist catastrophe bond and insurance bond investment manager Plenum Investment’s Index, which tracks this cat bond fund sector back to 2011. While catastrophe bond pricing has fallen from the high levels seen during the reinsurance hard market, catastrophe bond funds continue to deliver an attractive return for their investors in 2026. Of course, the lack of any major natural catastrophe loss events has helped considerably, but the returns are still historically attractive and well-above the average in 2026 so far. The latest data from the Plenum Index is for the period September 25th through October 31st 2026 and across this period the average return of the UCITS catastrophe bond funds reached 1.12%. Through 2026 so far, for the closest reported figures to calendar months, UCITS cat bond funds have returned: 0.53% for January 0.46% for February 0.35% for March 0.55% for April 0.36% for May 0.62% for June to the 26th of the month 1.15% for the subsequent period to July 31st 1.24% on average to August 28th 1.23% to September 25th and now 1.12% on average through to October 31st. As a result, the average year-to-date performance of the UCITS catastrophe bond fund strategies rose from 6.67% as of September 25th’s data, to now 7.87% as of October 31st 2026. You can analyse the Plenum CAT Bond UCITS Fund Indices in our charts: The UCITS catastrophe bond sector continues to track towards one of its best performing years on record, with the current figure of 7.87% YTD still the fourth best since 2011, when this Index began. Given the softening of reinsurance pricing and how that has reduced spreads in new cat bond issuance, future returns may not live up to the past. This is evident in a further decrease in the rolling twelve month return of the UCITS cat bond funds. The rolling twelve month return of this catastrophe bond fund index stood at 9.66% as of September 25th, but by October 31st has declined further to an average of 9.23%. Through this latest reporting period of record, from September 25th to October 31st 2026, while the average return of all the UCITS catastrophe bond funds reached 1.12%, the lower-risk cohort averaged 0.99% and the higher-risk group of cat bond funds averaged 1.20%, showing how different strategies have their own return profiles. On a capital-weighted basis the index return was 1.14% for the same period. On a year-to-date basis to October 31st, the average performance across the cat bond fund Index of 7.87% compares to the lower-risk UCITS cat bond funds now averaging 7.56%, while the higher-risk funds average 8.05% and the capital weighted Index stands at 8.10%. The rolling twelve month return of the average UCITS cat bond fund has declined slightly to 9.23% as we said, while for the lower-risk cat bond funds in this Index it declined to 8.93% and for the higher-risk funds it fell to 9.38%, while on a capital weighted basis it stands at 9.49%. As we explained though, while cat bond fund returns are lower this year, they still remain at a historically attractive level for catastrophe bond investors. The closest comparable 12-month period of the prior year saw the average rolling-twelve month return of UCITS catastrophe bonds funds standing at 10.99%.
